cues.text: A girl who loved football
Alexia Putellas was born in 1994 in Mollet del Vallès, near Barcelona.
She often travelled with her father to watch Barcelona play at the Camp Nou.
Alexia loved playing football at school, but back then she did not believe a girl could make football her job.
Open the school gate.
Her mother let her join a team only if she stopped playing at school.
Alexia later said this showed how society was unfair to girls who played football.
But she said her family always accepted her dreams, and she kept on playing.
Nobody gets to decide that a dream is not for you. Stay close to the people who believe in you.
Small, but finding space
At seven, Alexia tried a local boys’ team, but she trained there only three times, because she did not like the feeling there.
She joined the girls’ team at Sabadell instead.
She was younger, smaller and weaker than many teammates, and she could not yet shoot from far away.
That frustrated her.
Slide the ball into the space.
Writers said Alexia found space where there was none.
She was even made a team captain.
Getting her to training was hard for her family, but by 2004 she was playing all the time.
If a place doesn’t feel right, it’s okay to look for a better one. Small can still find a way.
The door that closed
In 2005, Alexia’s dream came true.
She joined a Barcelona girls’ youth team, and together they won their league.
But the next year, the club changed its girls’ teams, and there was no team left for her age group.
She had to leave.
Open the door to the new club.
At twelve, Alexia joined Espanyol, the other club in Barcelona, along with many other girls who had to leave.
She kept learning there, and at sixteen she played for Espanyol’s first team.
Xavi Llorens, who later coached Barcelona, said he always expected her to return.
When one door closes, keep going. A setback isn’t the end of the story.
Her biggest fan
At seventeen, Alexia moved to the club Levante, in Valencia, far from home.
Her father was ill with heart problems, but he still travelled to Valencia again and again to watch her play.
Alexia even thought about studying medicine to help him.
In 2012, just before a big youth tournament with Spain, her father died.
Light the star for her dad.
Less than a month later, Alexia still went to the tournament, and she was Spain’s captain.
She later said that football was her escape, and also her connection to her father.
It’s okay to feel very sad when you lose someone. Doing the things you shared can help you feel close to them.
Fingers to the sky
In the summer of 2012, after her father died, Barcelona asked Alexia to come back, and she signed on 10 July.
The next year she won her first league title with them.
When she scores, Alexia often points her fingers to the sky, for her father.
Lift the flap to see who she thanks.
In 2021, Alexia won the Ballon d’Or, one of the biggest prizes in football.
She dedicated it to her father and thanked her teammates.
One of her tattoos shows her father holding her as a baby, and handing her a football.
The people we love stay part of our story. You can keep them close in your own way.
The long way back
On 5 July 2022, the day before the European Championship began, Alexia badly hurt her left knee in training.
She needed an operation and almost a year to recover, and she watched Spain’s first match from the stands.
She later called it one of her lowest points.
Climb the steps back, one at a time.
While she healed, Alexia began planning a way to help girls play football, which became her Eleven Foundation.
In 2023 she played again, and that summer she came on in the World Cup final as Spain won.
Getting better can take a long time. Small steps count, and helping others can help you heal too.
